title: Resident fingerprinting and memory-bandwidth correlation probe
content:
Summary:
This is a working note for an experiment that tries to link fine-grained resident-set "fingerprints" to short-term memory-bandwidth pressure and paging/eviction activity on our serving machines. The goal is to understand whether small changes in the set of resident KV pages (fingerprint changes) precede or co-occur with measurable BW spikes and to identify micro-patterns that predict tail latency regressions.

Motivation / hypothesis:
- We see intermittent tail latency spikes during mixed tenant workloads where overall occupancy looks stable.
- Hypothesis: small churn in the top-X hot fragments (not visible in coarse hit-rate metrics) causes repeated DMA reads/PCIe traffic that drives short bandwidth bursts and eviction cascades.
- If we can fingerprint page-level residency and detect rapid fingerprint divergence, we might predict near-term BW spikes and preemptively adjust batching/prefetch.

High-level approach:
1) Continuous lightweight fingerprinting: sample residency bitmap per shard at 200ms intervals and compute a compact fingerprint (64-bit rolling hash) per shard/worker.
2) Correlate fingerprint delta (Hamming distance or bit-diff of rolling hash) with hardware counters: memory controller BW, PCIe read bytes, NVMe swap IO, and kernel pagein/pageout counts.
3) Tag trace windows by model name, sequence length percentile, and tenant-id to separate workload regimes.
4) Run synthetic and production-shadow workloads to validate whether fingerprint deltas lead or lag BW signals.

Instrumentation details:
- Fingerprint implementation: xxhash64 on a sorted list of resident page IDs for each logical shard; we store last 16 fingerprints in a circular buffer.
- Sampling cadence: 200ms baseline; 50ms subtraces for suspected anomalies. Tradeoffs: lower cadence reduces noise but loses short bursts.
- Counters collected: GPU memory controller (SMEM) BW (GB/s), PCIe read/write bytes/s, pcie-latency-95, kernel pagefaults/sec, swap read MB/s.
- Tracing: lightweight JSON event per sample (shard, ts, fingerprint, footprint_bytes, resident_pages_count, local_reuse_rate_estimate). Events are shipped to kinesis-internal and joined with prometheus at analysis stage.

Experiment setup:
- Machines: 8x A100-80GB (dedicated lab cluster), kernel 6.4, numactl and CPU pinning consistent with production serving config.
- Workloads:
  * S1: long-context chat emulator (seqlen 4096, batch=1–4)
  * S2: short completions mix (seqlen 64, QPS scaled to create contention)
  * S3: mixed multi-tenant replay (10 tenants, skewed hot keys)
- Duration: 3 runs x 30 minutes per workload.
- Baselines: existing kv-residency and evict-rate telemetry (for comparison).

Key findings (early, exploratory):
- Fingerprint divergence metric (Fdiv) often spikes 300–800ms before measured PCIe read throughput increases. Median lead time ~420ms in S3 runs.
- Spearman rho between 1s-aggregated Fdiv and PCIe-read-95 was 0.62 across all mixed-tenant runs (note: non-linear and workload-dependent).
- In S1 (long context), Fdiv was low but small deltas corresponded with micro-bursts in NVMe swap reads: interpretation is that large KV pages partially evict and are partially re-requested when sequence lengths cross token boundaries.
- Top-5% of fingerprint-delta events account for ~54% of observed tail-latency spikes in S3 (tail defined as >95th percentile request latency).
- When we artificially pinned the top 10% resident pages for a shard, observed BW spikes reduced and tail latencies improved by ~12% (single-run, need repeat).

Microbenchmarks / sanity checks:
- Verified fingerprint collision rate on synthetic datasets: ~1e-9 collisions per sample window for xxhash64 given our distribution (ok).
- Sampling overhead: ~0.8% CPU on worker processes at 200ms cadence; 50ms cadence ~2.6% cpu. Acceptable for lab but need light-mode for production.

Anomalies / noise sources noted:
- Garbage collection events (Python GC in some runners) cause spikes in resident-set enumeration; correlate and filter by process-GC flag.
- Kernel readahead and background pager activity occasionally create false positives; need to mask when swap IO backlog < 4MB/s.
- Multi-socket NUMA effects: cross-node DMA stalls amplify bandwidth signals; add node-local bandwidth counters to disambiguate.

Immediate next steps / action items:
- [Ravi] Harden the fingerprint sampling code to skip when worker is in GC (SRV-3487 followup).
- [Evelyn] Run 10x repeat runs of S3 with pinned-top-10 experiment to get confidence intervals (target 2025-11-12).
- Add a cheap sketch variant (bloom filter signature) to compare sensitivity vs. hash fingerprint (if bloom is cheaper, we can use 50ms cadence).
- Build a lightweight anomaly rule: if Fdiv_rate > threshold && PCIe_read_increase > X% then trigger temporary cache pin for top-N pages for 1s. Put as canary config behind feature flag.

Questions / open hypotheses:
- Is the primary driver of BW spikes repeated streaming reads (evictions followed by remote fetches) or is it unfortunate interleaving of background compsaction + reader bursts? Need to capture per-page origin (local memory vs swap vs remote).
- How stable are top hot fragment sets across tenants? If hot sets rotate faster than our pin window, pinning could increase fragmentation.

Artifacts / scripts:
- sampling code: github PR (see linked_artifacts) — contains fast enumerator and xxhash64 wrapper.
- analysis notebook: s3://redwood-labs/kv-fingerprint/analysis-notebook-20251103.ipynb (internal).
- dashboard panels added: kv_fingerprint.delta_rate, kv_fingerprint.top_changes, pcie.read_bytes_rate, kernel.swap_mb_read.

Notes to self (informal):
- This is exploratory. Don't jump to production automation without robust false-positive controls.
- Need to run on a narrower variety of instance types (V100, L40) to guarantee portability across Dedicated offerings.

Rough command examples used in lab:
- Run sampler: ./tools/kv-fingerprint-sampler --cadence 200ms --shard all --out /tmp/fp-events.json
- Join with metrics: python tools/join_fp_with_prom.py /tmp/fp-events.json --prom-query 'pcie_read_bytes' --window 1s

Slack thread / context: #serving-runtime (see pinned message 11/03/2025) — will post summary and ask platform team for NIC-level counters.

Conclusion (tentative):
Fingerprint divergence appears to be a promising signal for short-term BW pressure that correlates with tail latencies in mixed-tenant workloads. Next round should validate statistical significance and test lightweight sketch alternatives for production viability.

-- Maya
